crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Judicial Analytics
children.blurb: Judicial analytics is the use of data and statistical or machine learning methods to study how courts and judges behave, covering questions such as how long a case may take, how often a motion is granted, how a judge has ruled on similar issues, and how likely a given outcome is.

children.name: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
children.blurb: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns is the branch of litigation prediction that studies who is on the other side and how a case moves through the court, rather than what the law says.

children.name: Settlement Valuation and Risk
children.blurb: Settlement Valuation and Risk covers the analytical work of estimating what a case is likely to resolve for and how much uncertainty surrounds that number.

children.name: Jury Selection and Public Data
children.blurb: Jury selection and public data covers the use of openly available records to understand the pool from which a jury is drawn and to prepare for questioning during voir dire.

children.name: Live Testimony Cross-Referencing
children.blurb: Live testimony cross-referencing is the practice of matching what a witness says in court, in a deposition, or at a hearing against a body of prior statements, transcripts, exhibits, and filings as the words are spoken.

sections.body: Litigation prediction and judicial analytics is the use of data about courts, judges, lawyers and juries to estimate how a case is likely to move and how it might end. In practice, teams build models from docket entries, written opinions, hearing transcripts and public records, then use them to score motions, forecast timelines and compare possible outcomes. Judicial analytics looks at a judge's past rulings on similar issues, while opposing counsel analytics looks at how a firm or attorney tends to litigate. Settlement valuation turns those signals into ranges rather than single numbers, and jury work uses public data to reason about how a pool might respond to evidence. Live testimony cross-referencing links what a witness says in the moment to earlier statements in depositions, affidavits or prior hearings.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is partly mature and partly speculative. Docket and opinion data are widely available, and text models can classify rulings and extract patterns with reasonable reliability, so questions like how often a judge grants a particular kind of motion are now answerable in many jurisdictions. Settlement valuation is harder because outcomes depend on facts, negotiation and local practice that records rarely capture, so models produce ranges and scenarios, not verdicts. Jury work is the weakest area: public data is thin, and what a jury will do cannot be read from demographics alone. Live cross-referencing is technically feasible but sensitive to transcription errors, accents and courtroom audio, and any output still needs a human to judge relevance and admissibility. The honest limit across all of it is that prediction describes past patterns, not what a specific judge or jury will decide next.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from the bench outward to the courtroom floor. Judicial Analytics is the starting point, covering how rulings and opinions are read for patterns, and it feeds the assumptions used elsewhere. Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns shifts the lens to the other side, looking at filing habits and procedural timing. Settlement Valuation and Risk takes both streams and turns them into ranges and scenarios for negotiation. Jury Selection and Public Data deals with the thinnest evidence base, where public records are used cautiously to think about jury composition and response. Live Testimony Cross-Referencing is the most immediate page, about matching spoken testimony to the record as it happens. A reader would go to the first for judge behavior, the second for adversary behavior, the third for numbers, the fourth for jury questions and the fifth for real-time checking.
